feedback: Praise descriptions that name the shape of the pattern (belt, chain, high-to-low flow) before naming any cause.
If the learner reads a single data source and declares no pattern, ask them to add the overlay and look again.
If a learner reads river direction incorrectly, point back to the colour/elevation key to confirm water runs from high ground to low.
activities.intendedInsight: Real map data carries the pattern; combining data sources (physical overlays) can expose coincidences that a single map does not make obvious.
learnerActions: Use a real atlas or relief map (where colour shows elevation) and locate mountain chains and the direction rivers run from high to low ground.
Place a printed transparent overlay of volcano/earthquake locations on top of a physical world map.
Describe aloud what coincides when the overlay is in place.
Compare: how does the physical overlay experience differ from reading a single map on its own?
activities.title: Hands-on atlas and printed overlays

feedback: For a 'random' answer on a clearly belted map, ask the learner to trace the belt and reconsider.
For river tracing, confirm flow runs from high ground to low; if reversed, revisit relief/elevation reading.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a pattern and linking it to a process are distinct skills; a correct reading connects the arrangement to a cause acting over long time.
learnerActions: Read a volcano/earthquake map and identify the pattern shown (e.g. clustered in a belt vs scattered at random).
Match each observed pattern to its likely process (mountain chains ↔ plate collision/uplift; volcano/quake belts ↔ plate boundaries; valley shape ↔ erosion).
Trace a river's high-to-low course and a quake belt on a map.
activities.title: Pattern → process matching and tracing checks

feedback: Full reasoning: reads the pattern AND explains it as the signature of processes over long time, and can transfer (predicts a random map or reasons about river direction).
Partial: identifies belts and high-to-low rivers but stops short of linking them to processes over time — prompt 'what made them line up, and over how long?'
Gap: sees no pattern or calls the arrangement coincidence — confront by tracing the belts and comparing with plate-boundary locations to show they coincide.
If the learner explains a whole belt by one flood or one eruption, contrast a rapid one-off event with cumulative slow processes repeating over millions of years.
If the learner says features 'have just always been there', link to erosion and plate movement and use rock layers as evidence of change.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-random pattern is evidence that features form from Earth processes (plate movement, volcanism, erosion) acting in particular places over very long periods — not by chance, and not from a single dramatic one-off event.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'Most volcanoes and mountain chains line up in long belts, but a classmate says they are just scattered about randomly.'
State who is right and explain what the pattern tells you about how the features formed.

Answer the probes: Is the volcano belt a line or scattered, and what could line them up? Why do rivers run from higher ground down to lower ground (often ending at the sea or a lake), never uphill? If features formed by chance, what would the map look like instead? How long did a mountain chain take to build — a day or millions of years — and what is your evidence?
Describe what a truly random map would look like as a contrast.
activities.title: Argue the pattern: random or not?
